Duncan. The rightful King of Scotland in William Shakespeare's Macbeth, a virtuous and ineffectual ruler whose murder by Macbeth and Lady Macbeth sets the tragic action of the play in motion. Though he appears only briefly before his assassination, Duncan's character—honest, trusting, and beloved—defines the moral order that Macbeth's ambition destroys. He is a beloved king whose gentle rule has earned him the affection of his nobles, including Macbeth, whom he favours and trusts implicitly. His goodness and wisdom make him unaware of the depths of ambition and malice in those around him; he cannot imagine that Macbeth would betray him. Macbeth becomes thane of Cawdor and then receives a prophecy that he will be king, but Duncan's life stands in the way of this prophecy. Duncan's decision to name his son Malcolm as his successor precipitates Macbeth's decisive turn toward murder. His murder is portrayed with particular horror: he is killed while a guest in Macbeth's home, a violation of the sacred duty of hospitality. Duncan's blood cannot be washed from Macbeth's hands; his murder haunts Macbeth throughout the play, emblematic of how the crime against innocence can never be undone. Duncan's murder is not merely regicide but a violation of both the natural and divine law, making his death the catalyst that unleashes the horror that consumes Macbeth and Scotland. His son Malcolm, named heir, will eventually survive and restore order, mirroring the play's moral arc. Banquo, Duncan's kinsman and friend, remains loyal and his suspicions about Macbeth foreshadow the king's doom.
